name: Data and maths foundations
description: Python data handling, plots, probability, sampling and linear algebra: what you need before you model anything.

terms.definition: A table held in memory, with named columns of one type each and one row per observation; pandas in Python, data.frame in R.
terms.example: Each row of our data frame is one word, with its speaker, start time, end time and label.
terms.misuse: A data frame is not a spreadsheet: formulas do not live in cells, so every change is a line of code you can rerun.
terms.when: Use it when you describe how your data is stored and processed.

terms.definition: A table laid out so that each variable is a column, each observation a row and each kind of observational unit its own table.
terms.example: We reshaped the transcripts into tidy data: one row per word, never one row per speaker with words in columns.
terms.misuse: Tidy does not mean clean; a tidy table can still hold errors.
terms.when: Use it when you plan the shape of a table before analysis.

terms.definition: Applying an operation to a whole column or array at once instead of looping over items one by one.
terms.example: Pause length is a vectorised subtraction: start times minus the previous word's end times.
terms.misuse: Vectorised code is faster, but it is not automatically correct; check the first rows by hand.
terms.when: Use it when you explain why an analysis script runs in seconds rather than hours.

terms.definition: Looking at data with counts, summaries and plots before testing anything, to learn its shape, errors and surprises.
terms.example: Exploratory data analysis showed that three speakers produce half of all repetitions.
terms.misuse: Patterns found while exploring are ideas to test, not findings to report as confirmed.
terms.when: Use it for the first pass over any new data set.

terms.definition: A plot that splits a numeric variable into bins and shows how many values fall into each.
terms.example: The histogram of pause lengths has a long right tail.
terms.misuse: The picture changes with the bin width; try more than one before you describe a shape.
terms.when: Use it to see the distribution of one numeric variable.

terms.definition: A distribution with a longer tail on one side, so the mean is pulled away from the median.
terms.example: Pause durations are right-skewed: most are short, a few are very long.
terms.misuse: Skew is not an error in the data; it is often how durations and counts naturally behave.
terms.when: Use it when the mean and median of a variable disagree.

terms.definition: The middle value when the data is sorted; half the values lie below it and half above.
terms.example: The median pause before a fluent word was 180 ms.
terms.misuse: The median is not a better mean in every case; with symmetric data both tell the same story.
terms.when: Use it to summarise skewed data such as durations.

terms.definition: Replacing each value with its logarithm, which turns multiplicative differences into additive ones and pulls in long right tails.
terms.example: We modelled log pause duration, so an effect means a percentage change in pause length.
terms.misuse: A logged variable changes how you read coefficients; say so when you report them.
terms.when: Use it for positive, right-skewed measures such as durations and frequencies.

terms.definition: A quantity whose value depends on chance, described by the probabilities of its possible values.
terms.example: Whether the next word is stuttered can be treated as a random variable with two values.
terms.misuse: Random does not mean without cause; it means we describe it with probabilities.
terms.when: Use it when you set up a probability model of your data.

terms.definition: A description of how likely each possible value of a random variable is.
terms.example: A language model gives a probability distribution over the next word.
terms.misuse: A distribution of observed values in a sample is an estimate of the true one, not the thing itself.
terms.when: Use it when you talk about what values are likely and how likely.

terms.definition: The probability of an event given that another has happened, written P(A | B).
terms.example: Surprisal uses the probability of a word given the words before it.
terms.misuse: P(A | B) is not P(B | A): the chance of a stutter given a long word differs from the chance of a long word given a stutter.
terms.when: Use it whenever a probability depends on context.

terms.definition: The rule that turns P(B | A) into P(A | B) using how common A and B are on their own.
terms.example: Bayes' rule explains why a detector that is right 95% of the time still raises many false alarms when stutters are rare.
terms.misuse: Using it well needs a sensible base rate; a guessed one gives a confident wrong answer.
terms.when: Use it when you reason from evidence back to causes, or about rare events.

terms.definition: The power a base must be raised to in order to give a number; log2(8) is 3.
terms.example: Multiplying probabilities along a sentence becomes adding their logarithms.
terms.misuse: Say which base you used: bits for base 2, nats for base e.
terms.when: Use it for probabilities, durations and anything that grows by multiplying.

terms.definition: The logarithm of a probability, always zero or negative; the negative of it is surprisal.
terms.example: A word with probability 1/8 has a log2 probability of -3, so a surprisal of 3 bits.
terms.misuse: Small differences in log probability can be large differences in probability; read them on the log scale.
terms.when: Use it whenever you work with probabilities from a model.

terms.definition: The distribution a statistic, such as a mean, would have if you drew many samples of the same size.
terms.example: The sampling distribution of mean pause length tells us how much it would move with a different set of speakers.
terms.misuse: It is not the distribution of your data; it is the distribution of a number computed from the data.
terms.when: Use it when you explain where standard errors and confidence intervals come from.

terms.definition: Estimating uncertainty by resampling your own data with replacement many times and recomputing the statistic each time.
terms.example: We bootstrapped by speaker, so each resample kept a speaker's words together.
terms.misuse: Resample the unit you want to generalise to; resampling words when you care about speakers makes you overconfident.
terms.when: Use it for uncertainty when no simple formula fits.

terms.definition: As a sample grows, its average gets closer to the true average.
terms.example: With 3,000 segments the overall disfluency rate is stable, but one speaker's rate from 20 words is not.
terms.misuse: It says nothing about small samples, and it does not make a biased sample unbiased.
terms.when: Use it to explain why small groups give noisy numbers.

terms.definition: An ordered list of numbers; it can describe one observation's features or a direction in space.
terms.example: Each word becomes a vector: length, frequency, position and surprisal.
terms.misuse: In machine learning a vector is often just a list of numbers; the arrow picture is an aid, not a requirement.
terms.when: Use it when you describe inputs, weights or embeddings.

terms.definition: A rectangular grid of numbers; a data set with rows of observations and columns of features is one.
terms.example: Our design matrix has one row per word and one column per predictor.
terms.misuse: Rows and columns are not interchangeable; mixing them up breaks every multiplication.
terms.when: Use it when you describe data or a model's weights in bulk.

terms.definition: Multiply two vectors element by element and add the results; it measures how much they point the same way.
terms.example: A linear model's prediction is the dot product of a word's features with the weights.
terms.misuse: A large dot product can come from long vectors, not only similar ones; cosine similarity corrects for length.
terms.when: Use it when you explain how a linear model or an embedding comparison works.

terms.definition: Combining two matrices by taking the dot product of each row of the first with each column of the second.
terms.example: Multiplying the design matrix by the weight vector gives every word's prediction at once.
terms.misuse: Order matters: A times B is usually not B times A, and the inner sizes must match.
terms.when: Use it when you explain how models process many examples at once.

lessons.title: Python for data: NumPy and pandas
lessons.why: Almost every research project starts by loading, cleaning and reshaping tables; doing it in code makes every step checkable and repeatable.

read.title: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners

lessons.do: Load a table with one row per word (speaker, word, start time, end time, label). Count words and labels per speaker with groupby, add a column for each word's duration, and save the result as a new file from a script you can rerun.
lessons.speak: In one minute, explain why each row is one word and not one speaker, and what that choice lets you do.
lessons.check: Does rerunning the script from the raw file give exactly the same table, and did you check five rows by hand?

lessons.title: Looking at data before modelling it
lessons.why: Plots and simple summaries catch errors, outliers and odd speakers before they quietly shape a result.

read.title: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, 2nd edition, chapter 1
read.by: Peter Bruce, Andrew Bruce and Peter Gedeck

lessons.do: Plot a histogram of pause lengths between words, then the same on a log scale. Report the mean and the median, and list the three speakers with the most and fewest disfluencies per 100 words.
lessons.speak: Describe the shape of the pause distribution in plain words, and say why the median is the better summary here.
lessons.check: Did you look for impossible values (negative pauses, zero-length words) and decide what to do with them before going on?

lessons.title: Probability you will actually use
lessons.why: Language models, classifiers and statistical tests all speak in probabilities; surprisal is just a log probability turned round.

read.title: Seeing Theory: basic probability and compound probability

lessons.do: In Python, estimate from your table the probability that a word is disfluent overall and given that it is a speaker's first word in a segment. Then take five probabilities (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/100, 1/1000) and compute their surprisal in bits.
lessons.speak: Explain surprisal to a friend in two sentences, using the idea of how unexpected a word is.
lessons.check: Can you say in words the difference between P(disfluent | first word) and P(first word | disfluent)?

lessons.title: Samples, uncertainty and the bootstrap
lessons.why: Any number from a sample would change with a different sample; research reports say how much.

read.title: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, 2nd edition, chapter 2
read.by: Peter Bruce, Andrew Bruce and Peter Gedeck

lessons.do: Bootstrap the median pause length 2,000 times, first resampling words, then resampling whole speakers. Report both 95% intervals and explain why they differ.
lessons.speak: In one minute, explain why resampling speakers gives a wider interval, and which one you would report.
lessons.check: Is the unit you resampled the same unit you want your conclusion to be about?

lessons.title: Linear algebra for data
lessons.why: A data set is a matrix and a linear model is a matrix times a vector; seeing that makes every later model easier.

read.title: Essence of linear algebra, chapters 1 to 4

lessons.do: Build a small matrix with one row per word and three columns (length in letters, position in the segment, a constant 1). Pick a weight vector by hand and compute every word's prediction with one matrix multiplication in NumPy, then with a loop, and confirm they match.
lessons.speak: Explain in one minute how one matrix multiplication makes a prediction for every row at once.
lessons.check: Can you state the shapes of the matrix, the weights and the result, and why they must fit?

lessons.title: An end-to-end project, start to finish
lessons.why: Seeing a whole project once (question, data, checks, model, evaluation) shows where each skill fits before you learn them in depth.

read.title: Hands-On Machine Learning, 2nd edition, chapters 1 and 2
Notebooks for Hands-On Machine Learning, 2nd edition

lessons.do: Work through the chapter 2 notebook yourself. Then write a one-page data check note for your own data set: where it came from, its licence, what one row means, missing values, odd speakers, and what you will and will not use.
lessons.speak: Walk someone through your data check note in two minutes as if they were your supervisor.
lessons.check: Would a stranger be able to rebuild your table from the raw download using only your note and your script?
